content: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) is a key agency within the United States Department of Health and Human Services, tasked with overseeing and conducting biomedical research. It is the primary federal entity responsible for advancing medical knowledge and innovation. Approximately 28% of the total annual biomedical research funding in the United States, equating to about $28 billion, is allocated through the NIH, with the remainder largely coming from private industry. The NIH operates through two main divisions: the Extramural division, which funds research conducted outside of the NIH, and the Intramural division, which conducts research internally. Intramural research is primarily carried out at the NIH's main campus in Bethesda, Maryland, as well as in surrounding areas. Additional facilities include the National Institute on Aging and the National Institute on Drug Abuse in Baltimore, Maryland, and the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences in Research Triangle, North Carolina. The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases also operates the Rocky Mountain Laboratories in Hamilton, Montana, focusing on virology. The NIH traces its origins back to 1887, when it was established as the Laboratory of Hygiene. It was reorganized in 1930 under the Ransdell Act, becoming the National Institute of Health (singular at the time). Today, the NIH is recognized as one of the world's leading medical research institutions and serves as the federal government's focal point for medical research in the United States. The NIH is composed of 27 distinct institutes and centers, as well as the Office of the Director. Its mission is to generate new knowledge aimed at preventing, detecting, diagnosing, and treating diseases and disabilities, ranging from rare genetic disorders to common illnesses like the cold. The NIH achieves this mission by conducting research in its own laboratories, funding external research at universities, medical schools, hospitals, and research institutions both domestically and internationally, training research investigators, and promoting the dissemination of medical and health science information. The NIH is organized into various institutes, each focusing on specific areas of research. These include the National Cancer Institute (NCI), the National Eye Institute (NEI), the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), the National Institute on Aging (NIA), the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIBIB), the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD), the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR), the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS), the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS), the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), the National Institute of Nursing Research (NINR), and the National Library of Medicine (NLM). In addition to its institutes, the NIH also includes several centers that support its mission. These include the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), the Center for Information Technology (CIT), the Center for Scientific Review (CSR), the John E. Fogarty International Center (FIC), the National Center for Complementary and Alternative Medicine (NCCAM), the National Center on Minority Health and Health Disparities (NCMHD), the National Center for Research Resources (NCRR), the Quality Assurance Review Center (QARC), the Warren Grant Magnuson Clinical Center (CC), and the Radiological Physics Center (RPC). The Office of the Director (OD) serves as the central administrative body of the NIH. It is responsible for setting policies, planning, managing, and coordinating the programs and activities of all NIH components. The OD includes several program offices that focus on specific research areas, such as minority health, women's health, AIDS research, disease prevention, and behavioral and social sciences research. These offices also provide funding to support research initiatives across the NIH institutes. Key offices within the OD include: Office of Extramural Research (OER): Provides guidance for research and training programs conducted through grants, contracts, and cooperative agreements. Office of Intramural Research (OIR): Oversees research conducted directly by NIH personnel. Office of Management (OM): Manages financial and administrative functions of the NIH. Office of Administration (OA): Advises on administrative policies and oversees areas such as information resources, grant administration, procurement, and logistics. Office of AIDS Research (OAR): Develops scientific policies and allocates resources for AIDS research. Office of Behavioral and Social Sciences Research (OBSSR): Advises on research related to human behavior and its impact on health and disease prevention. Office of Communications and Public Liaison (OCPL): Communicates NIH policies, programs, and research findings to the public. Office of Community Liaison (OCL): Promotes collaboration between the NIH and its surrounding community. Office of Disease Prevention (ODP): Coordinates research applications in disease prevention, nutrition, and medical practice. Office of Intramural Training and Education (OITE): Provides resources for postdoctoral training opportunities at the NIH. Office of Equal Opportunity and Diversity Management (OEODM): Advises on equal employment opportunity programs and policies. Office of Financial Management (OFM): Oversees financial management, budget preparation, and fund allocation. Office of Human Resources (OHR): Manages human resource services and planning. Office of Portfolio Analysis and Strategic Initiatives (OPASI): Identifies emerging scientific opportunities and public health challenges, facilitating investments in these areas. Office of Research on Women's Health (ORWH): Office of Science Education (OSE): Develops science education programs and resources for students, teachers, and the public, including curriculum supplements and career exploration tools. The NIH is a cornerstone of biomedical research in the United States, driving advancements in health and medicine through its comprehensive network of institutes, centers, and offices.
